text: A psalm of David. Ascribe to the LORD, you heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.
Ascribe to the LORD the glory of his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness.
The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders, the LORD over the mighty waters.
The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty.

versions.text: The voice of the LORD is power; the voice of the LORD is majesty.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses the preposition beth ("with power... with majesty"), describing the manner of the voice rather than equating the voice with the abstract nouns. "The voice is power" reads awkwardly aloud; the adjectival rendering is both more accurate and more natural for oral reading.

text: The voice of the LORD shatters the cedars; the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon.
He makes them skip like a calf, Lebanon and Sirion like a young wild ox.

versions.text: He makes Lebanon skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb carries a third-person plural suffix ("he makes them skip"), referring back to the cedars of verse 5, with Lebanon and Sirion then named. The current wording loses the connection to the shattered cedars.

text: The voice of the LORD flashes forth flames of fire.

versions.text: The voice of the LORD strikes out flames of fire.
versions.explanation: The participle means "hews" or "cleaves out," pictured here as lightning splitting the sky. "Strikes out" is ambiguous in English (it can mean "fails" or "deletes"); "flashes forth" conveys the image clearly and reads better aloud.

text: The voice of the LORD makes the wilderness tremble; the LORD makes the wilderness of Kadesh tremble.
The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth and strips the forests bare. And in his temple all cry, "Glory!"
The LORD sits enthroned above the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever.
The LORD gives strength to his people; the LORD blesses his people with peace.
